1.context:
## Where This Chapter Fits

Genesis 1 opens the Bible, the Torah (the five books of Moses), and the **primeval history** of Genesis 1–11, which moves from creation to the scattering of nations before narrowing to Abraham in chapter 12. The literary unit actually runs from **1:1 to 2:3**: the seventh day belongs with the first six, and the chapter break after 1:31 was added in the Middle Ages (chapter divisions are usually credited to Stephen Langton, c. AD 1220s). A second, differently styled creation account begins at 2:4.

## Authorship and Date

The chapter itself names no author and gives no date.

- **Traditional view:** Jewish and Christian tradition attribute the Torah to Moses (13th or 15th century BC, depending on the dating of the Exodus).
- **Critical scholarship:** many scholars assign 1:1–2:3 to a "Priestly" (P) writer or school, usually dated to the exile or just after (6th–5th century BC), drawing on older traditions. Others argue for earlier dates or for a more unified composition. These remain hypotheses; no manuscript evidence directly settles the question.
- **Restoration perspective:** Moses 1–2 (revealed to Joseph Smith in 1830 during his inspired revision of the Bible) presents this creation account as a revelation given to Moses, framed by the Lord's words "write the words which I speak" (Moses 2:1). Abraham 4 offers a parallel account in which "the Gods" plan and organize the creation.

## Original Language and Key Terms

Genesis was written in **Biblical Hebrew**. A few words shape how the chapter is read:

- ***Bereshit*** ("In the beginning," v. 1) is the Hebrew name of the book. The word lacks the definite article, so v. 1 can be read as an independent statement ("In the beginning God created…") or as a time clause ("When God began to create…," as in the NRSV and JPS translations). The choice affects whether v. 2 describes a state *before* God's first act.
- ***Bara*** ("create," vv. 1, 21, 27) is used in the Hebrew Bible only with God as subject. Many Hebrew scholars note that the verb itself does not require creation out of nothing. Joseph Smith taught that the word means "to organize" existing material (King Follett Discourse, 1844), and Abraham 4 consistently uses "organized" and "formed."
- ***Elohim*** ("God") is plural in form but takes singular verbs here; it is the only divine name used in 1:1–2:3.
- ***Tohu wa-bohu*** ("without form, and void," v. 2) is a rhyming pair describing an empty, unproductive state; the rest of the chapter answers it.
- ***Tehom*** ("the deep," v. 2) is the primordial ocean. It is linguistically related to *Tiamat*, the sea-goddess of Babylonian myth, but in Genesis it is simply water, not a rival deity.
- ***Ruach elohim*** (v. 2) can mean "Spirit of God" or "wind of God"; *ruach* means breath, wind, and spirit.
- ***Raqia*** ("firmament," v. 6) comes from a verb meaning to beat or hammer out (like metal). It describes a solid-seeming dome or expanse separating waters above from waters below, as ancient Israelites perceived the sky. Abraham 4:6 renders it "expanse."
- ***Tselem*** and ***demut*** ("image" and "likeness," v. 26).

## The Ancient Near Eastern Setting

Genesis 1 was first heard in a world full of creation stories, and much of its meaning comes from how it differs from them.

- **Babylon:** In *Enuma Elish*, the god Marduk defeats the sea-goddess Tiamat and builds heaven and earth from her split corpse; humans are made from a slain god's blood to do the gods' labor. Genesis also separates waters above and below, but with no battle: God speaks, and it happens. Humans are not slaves but royal representatives who receive blessing (v. 28).
- **Egypt:** Memphite theology describes the god Ptah creating by thought and spoken word, which offers a partial parallel to creation by command.
- **The heavenly bodies:** On day four the sun and moon are not named, only "the greater light" and "the lesser light" (v. 16). In surrounding cultures the sun and moon were major deities (and the Hebrew words for them resemble divine names). Many interpreters see a quiet polemic here: they are lamps set in place to mark time, not gods to be worshiped.
- **The image of God:** Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts call the *king* the image of a god, and kings set up statues as their "image" in conquered lands. Genesis 1:26–27 gives that royal status to *all* humankind, male and female.

## Reading Approaches (Hermeneutics)

Readers have long disagreed about what kind of text Genesis 1 is, and the chapter supports several careful readings:

- **Literal-chronological:** six consecutive 24-hour days.
- **Day-age:** each "day" is a long period.
- **Literary or framework:** the days are a theological structure (see the Literary Unit tab) rather than a timeline.
- **Functional or cosmic-temple** (John Walton and others): the chapter describes God assigning functions and roles to the cosmos and taking up residence in it on the seventh day, the way a temple is dedicated.

**Latter-day Saint notes:** Abraham 4 calls each period a "time" (Abraham 4:8), and Abraham 5:13 refers to "the Lord's time" being different from human reckoning (see Abraham 3:4). Moses 3:5 adds that God created all things "spiritually" before they were naturally on the earth. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has taken no official position on the age of the earth or the length of the creative periods.

## Why It Matters

Genesis 1 sets out the Bible's foundational claims: one God creates by his word, the created world is repeatedly called "good" (seven times), humankind bears God's image, and the week ends in sacred rest. Later scripture builds directly on it. John 1:1–3 and Hebrews 11:3 return to creation by the word, Moses 2:1 names the Only Begotten as the one through whom God created, and in Moses 2:26 the "Let us" of v. 26 is addressed to him.

breakdown.title: The Beginning and the Unformed Earth
breakdown.summary: A headline statement of God creating heaven and earth, followed by the starting conditions: an earth *without form and void*, darkness over the deep, and the Spirit (or wind) of God moving over the waters.

breakdown.title: Day One: Light
breakdown.summary: God speaks light into being, calls it good, and separates it from darkness. He names them Day and Night, and the first evening-and-morning refrain closes the day.

breakdown.title: Day Two: The Firmament
breakdown.summary: God makes a firmament (expanse) to divide the waters above from the waters below and names it Heaven. This is the only day without the words "it was good."

breakdown.title: Day Three: Land, Seas, and Plants
breakdown.summary: The waters below are gathered so dry land appears, named Earth and Seas. In a second command the earth brings forth plants and fruit trees, each reproducing *after its kind*.

breakdown.title: Day Four: The Lights in the Heavens
breakdown.summary: God sets the greater and lesser lights and the stars in the firmament to divide day from night and to mark signs, seasons, days, and years. The lights are described by function, not by name.

breakdown.title: Day Five: Creatures of Sea and Sky
breakdown.summary: The waters teem with living creatures, including the great sea creatures, and birds fill the sky. For the first time God blesses what he made and commands it to be fruitful and multiply.

breakdown.title: Day Six (I): Land Animals
breakdown.summary: The earth brings forth cattle, creeping things, and wild beasts after their kinds, and God sees that it is good.

breakdown.title: Day Six (II): Humankind in God's Image
breakdown.summary: After a deliberative "Let us make man," God creates humankind, male and female, in his own image. He blesses them to multiply, fill and subdue the earth, and have dominion over living things.

breakdown.title: Day Six (III): Provision and "Very Good"
breakdown.summary: God gives plants and fruit as food for humans and animals. Surveying everything he has made, he declares it *very good*, and the sixth day closes. The seventh day of rest follows in 2:1-3, completing the account.

1.literaryUnit:
## Genre

Genesis 1 is **elevated prose narrative**. It is not Hebrew poetry in the strict sense (it lacks consistent line-by-line parallelism), but it is so rhythmic, repetitive, and carefully numbered that it reads almost like liturgy. The style is calm and declarative, with no conflict, dialogue partners, or drama, only command and fulfillment.

## Boundaries of the Unit

The unit is **1:1–2:3**, not chapter 1 alone. It is framed by an **inclusio**: "God created the heaven and the earth" (1:1) is answered by "the heavens and the earth were finished" and "which God created" (2:1–3). Genesis 2:4a ("These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth") either closes this account or opens the next. It is the first of the *toledot* ("generations") formulas that organize the whole book.

## Structure: Forming and Filling

Verse 2 names two problems: the earth is *formless* (*tohu*) and *empty* (*bohu*). The six days answer them in two matching sets of three:

- **Day 1** (light and darkness) is filled on **Day 4** (sun, moon, stars)
- **Day 2** (sky and waters) is filled on **Day 5** (birds and sea creatures)
- **Day 3** (dry land and plants) is filled on **Day 6** (land animals and humans)

Days 1–3 **form** the realms, and days 4–6 **fill** them.

Days 3 and 6 each contain **two** creative acts, so each triad ends with a double climax. **Day 7** stands outside the pattern entirely: nothing is made, and God rests and sanctifies the day.

## The Refrains

Each day is built from a recurring set of formulas, which makes small variations stand out:

1. **Announcement:** "And God said…"
2. **Command:** "Let there be…" / "Let the waters…"
3. **Fulfillment:** "and it was so"
4. **Action or naming:** God divides, makes, or calls
5. **Evaluation:** "God saw that it was good"
6. **Time marker:** "the evening and the morning were the … day"

**Notable departures:**

- Day 2 lacks "it was good."
- Day 6 escalates to "very good" (v. 31).
- Day 7 has no evening-and-morning refrain, which leaves God's rest open-ended.
- Naming happens in days 1–3, and **blessing** in days 5, 6, and 7.

## Patterns of Seven and Ten

The chapter is built around the number **seven**, the number of completion:

- v. 1 has **7** Hebrew words, and v. 2 has **14** (2 × 7).
- "God" (*Elohim*) occurs **35** times in 1:1–2:3 (5 × 7).
- "Good" occurs **7** times (vv. 4, 10, 12, 18, 21, 25, 31).
- The whole account culminates on the **seventh** day.

"And God said" occurs **ten** times (vv. 3, 6, 9, 11, 14, 20, 24, 26, 28, 29). Jewish tradition speaks of the world being created by "ten utterances" (Pirkei Avot 5:1).

## The Climax: Verse 27

The pace changes at v. 26. The impersonal "Let there be" gives way to a deliberative **"Let us make,"** and v. 27 breaks into a short **poetic triplet**, the most poetic moment of the chapter. The verb *bara* ("created") appears three times in a single verse:

- created man in his own image
- in the image of God created he him
- male and female created he them

The first two lines form a small **chiasm** (created / image // image / created). The third line adds a new element: humankind is male and female together.

## Key Word Patterns

- **"Divide/separate"** (vv. 4, 6, 7, 14, 18): creation as ordering by separation.
- **"After his kind"** (10 times in vv. 11–25): order and stability in living things.
- **"Light"/"darkness"**: introduced in day 1 and given rulers in day 4, which ties the two triads together.

## How the Chapter Reads as a Whole

The movement is from chaos to order, from emptiness to fullness, and from darkness to light. It ends not with humankind but with **rest and holiness**. The structure carries the theology: a sovereign God creates by word, the world is purposeful and good, humans are set within it as God's image-bearers, and the week culminates in sacred time.
